Get started

Source: vignettes/OECDscaleup.Rmd
OECDscaleup.Rmd

Development version. OECDscaleup is under active development, so functions and outputs may still change. Please report problems and suggestions as an issue on GitHub or to scaleup@oecd.org. Use synthetic data in a report (for example from example_scaleup_data()), never confidential firm data.

What OECDscaleup does

OECDscaleup computes indicators on high-growth firms (“scalers”) from national firm-level microdata, for the OECD Scale Up project, part of the OECD’s work to understand SMEs and their potential to scale up (see Helping SMEs scale up). It builds on previous OECD routines written in Stata. The firm-level data never leave the national statistical institute that holds them: the package produces aggregate tables, with the statistics needed to check them for confidentiality before they are shared.

It has three parts:

  • the baseline: a firm-year panel of indicators, and from it tables on the characteristics of scalers, what happens before and after scaling, their contribution to job and turnover creation, and the predictors of scaling;
  • the scaler analysis: the fastest-growing scalers, and scalers that grow into mid-caps;
  • trade (optional): exporters, importers and exporting scalers, from firm-level trade in goods.

Installation

The package is not on CRAN. Install it from GitHub with devtools:

# install.packages("devtools")
devtools::install_github("amannj/OECDscaleup", build_vignettes = TRUE)
library(OECDscaleup)

The workflow at a glance

This article goes through the whole analysis on fabricated data:

  1. Example data
  2. Configuration
  3. Check the inputs
  4. The indicator panel
  5. Characteristics of scalers
  6. Before and after scaling
  7. Contribution to job and turnover creation
  8. Predictors of scaling
  9. The scaler analysis
  10. Confidentiality
  11. Running everything from files
  12. Optional: trade

Steps 4 to 9 are functions that take data frames and return data frames. In production a country runs them from its files in one go (step 11). The input variables are described in vignette("input-data") and vignette("input-trade-data").

Step 1: Example data

example_scaleup_data() simulates the input files: a panel of firms with entries, exits, high-growth episodes and a few firms that grow past 250 employees, plus plants and trade flows. The data are random: none of the numbers below mean anything.

ex <- example_scaleup_data(n_firms = 3000, years = 2010:2022, seed = 1)
sapply(ex, nrow)
#> base_financials      plants_raw       trade_raw 
#>           25182           34335           43198
head(ex$base_financials[, 1:10])
#>   idf year birth_year sector_1d sector_2d sector_3d region_2d region_3d employment turnover
#> 1   1 2010       2009         C        26       261      FRB0     FRB06        2.7    250.6
#> 2   1 2011       2009         C        26       261      FRB0     FRB06        2.6    254.4
#> 3   2 2010       2007         C        25       251      FRB0     FRB04       10.2   1497.5
#> 4   2 2011       2007         C        25       251      FRB0     FRB04       10.4   1664.6
#> 5   2 2012       2007         C        25       251      FRB0     FRB04       10.7   1824.6
#> 6   2 2013       2007         C        25       251      FRB0     FRB04       10.7   1649.4

base_financials is the firm-level panel (one row per firm and year); plants_raw lists each firm’s plants, and trade_raw its trade flows (used in the optional trade part). Money is in EUR thousand.

Step 2: Configuration

Every function takes a configuration from config_scaleup():

cfg <- config_scaleup(
  country = "FR",
  input_dir = tempdir(),  # where the input files are (used in step 11)
  output_dir = tempdir(), # where the output tables go
  nace_revision = "2"     # NACE revision of the sector codes: "2" or "2.1"
)
  • nace_revision is required. A panel that switches from NACE Rev. 2 to Rev. 2.1 also gives nace_rev21_from, the first Rev. 2.1 year.
  • financials_unit = "EUR" declares money variables in euros instead of EUR thousand; the build then divides them by 1000.
  • dominance = TRUE adds the dominance statistics for the confidentiality checks (step 10).

Step 3: Check the inputs

check_inputs() compares the data with the variable dictionary before anything is computed. It lists errors (what would stop the build), warnings (what looks wrong or will be lost) and notes (what the build will do to the data). The report holds counts and shares only, so it can be shared.

chk <- check_inputs(cfg, ex$base_financials, ex$plants_raw, ex$trade_raw,
                    tl3_typology = tl3_typology)
#> Input check for FR: 0 error(s), 0 warning(s), 24 note(s); 31 check(s) ok.
#> 
#> Notes:
#>   base_financials$age                      absent (nice-to-have, second order; package: optional).
#>   base_financials$exit                     absent (nice-to-have, second order; package: optional).
#>   base_financials$exit_close               absent (nice-to-have, first order; package: not used).
#>   base_financials$exp_revenues_goods       absent (nice-to-have, second order; package: not used).
#>   base_financials$exp_revenues_services    absent (nice-to-have, second order; package: not used).
#>   base_financials$labour_costs             missing in 1,250 of 25,182 (5.0 %) rows.
#>   base_financials$operating_costs          absent (nice-to-have, second order; package: not used).
#>   base_financials$services_costs           absent (nice-to-have, first order; package: not used).
#>   base_financials$depr_amort               missing in 1,312 of 25,182 (5.2 %) rows.

#>   base_financials$total_assets             missing in 1,287 of 25,182 (5.1 %) rows.

#>   base_financials$profit_after_tax         absent (nice-to-have, second order; package: not used).
#>   base_financials$added_value              missing in 1,268 of 25,182 (5.0 %) rows.
#>   base_financials$cash_flow                missing in 1,300 of 25,182 (5.2 %) rows.
#>   base_financials$uco                      missing in 459 of 25,182 (1.8 %) rows.

No errors or warnings here. The notes list the optional variables the example does not have, and the firms in agriculture and finance, which the analysis leaves out.

Step 4: The indicator panel

build_accounts_indicators() cleans the panel and derives every indicator the tables use: growth rates, the scaler flags, size, age and sector classes, productivity and financial ratios.

ai <- build_accounts_indicators(cfg, ex$base_financials, ex$plants_raw,
                                tl3_typology = tl3_typology)
dim(ai)
#> [1] 24613    98

The scaler flags compare year t with year t-3:

Flag A firm with at least 10 employees at t-3 whose …
HGE20, HGE10 employment grew by more than 20 % (10 %) a year on average from t-3 to t
HGT20, HGT10 turnover grew by more than 20 % (10 %) a year on average
HGB20, HGB10 employment and turnover both did
HGET20, HGET10 employment or turnover did
MHGE20, MHGT20 the same, for micro firms (fewer than 10 employees at t-3)

Each flag is compared with its pool (HGE_pool, HGT_pool, …): the firms with at least 10 employees at t-3 whose growth is known. Breakdowns use the firm’s situation at t-3 (variables starting with L3): size class, age class, sector group, region, urban or rural region, independence, multi-plant and foreign ownership.

The share of employment scalers among the firms that could have scaled:

pool <- ai[ai$HGE_pool %in% 1, ]
round(100 * tapply(pool$HGE20, pool$year, mean), 1)
#> 2013 2014 2015 2016 2017 2018 2019 2020 2021 2022 
#>  2.3  4.3  4.1  3.7  3.6  3.7  4.7  4.8  4.5  4.4

Step 5: Characteristics of scalers

compute_characteristics() describes the scalers and the non-scalers of their pool, by year and breakdown: the number of firms, medians and means of size, growth, productivity and financial ratios at t-3 and at t, and shares (young, independent, multi-plant, foreign-owned).

ch <- compute_characteristics(cfg, ai)
x <- ch[ch$year == 2019 & ch$category == "ALL" &
          ch$sample %in% c("HGE20", "HGE20_nonscaler_pool"),
        c("sample", "firm_count", "median_L3employment", "median_employment",
          "median_employment_growth3y", "L3share_young")]
knitr::kable(x, digits = 2)
sample firm_count median_L3employment median_employment median_employment_growth3y L3share_young
HGE20 39 28.88 58.74 0.97 0.08
HGE20_nonscaler_pool 785 23.68 24.14 0.03 0.09

Rows are cells: sample is the group of firms, category and group the breakdown (ALL for all firms; for example L3size_cat and a size class). The medians are approximate medians, the average of the five central values, so that no single firm’s value is published.

Step 6: Before and after scaling

compute_persistence() follows scalers over time:

  • transitions: firms that scaled in 2014-2016, classified by what happened in the three years after (FOLLOW: high growth again, growing, stable, partial or full reversal, acquisition, missing information);
  • evolutions: firms that scaled in 2017, classified by the three years before (LEAD) and after.
pe <- compute_persistence(cfg, ai)
names(pe)
#> [1] "transitions"   "evolutions_p1" "evolutions_p2"
tr <- pe$transitions
x <- tr[tr$hg == "HGE20" & tr$category == "ALL" & tr$year == 2014 &
          !is.na(tr$FOLLOW) & is.na(tr$FOLLOW_othvar), c("year", "FOLLOW", "N_scalers")]
knitr::kable(x)
year FOLLOW N_scalers
2014 Missing info 4
2014 Partial reversal 1
2014 Stable 3
2014 Growing 13
2014 HG again 5

FOLLOW_othvar classifies the same firms by the other variable (turnover for employment scalers).

Step 7: Contribution to job and turnover creation

compute_contribution() splits the change in employment and turnover from t-3 to t into creation (firms that grew) and destruction (firms that shrank), by group of firms, for the years 2014, 2017 and 2019-2021.

co <- compute_contribution(cfg, ai)
p1 <- co$contribution_p1
jobs <- p1[p1$year == 2019 & p1$category == "ALL" & p1$type == "creation" &
             p1$variable == "employment", c("sample", "N_firms", "S3sum")]
jobs$share_of_creation <- round(100 * jobs$S3sum / jobs$S3sum[jobs$sample == "ALL"], 1)
knitr::kable(jobs[jobs$sample %in% c("ALL", "HGE20", "nonHGE20", "entrants"), ])
sample N_firms S3sum share_of_creation
ALL 1114 8932.0 100.0
HGE20 39 2047.0 22.9
nonHGE20 449 3703.7 41.5
entrants 238 1813.7 20.3

Step 8: Predictors of scaling

compute_predictors() classifies scalers by their position at t-3 among the firms of their sector and year (top quartile of productivity, capital intensity or wages, …) and estimates linear probability models of scaling on these predictors. It needs added_value, tangible_fixed_assets and labour_costs.

pr <- compute_predictors(cfg, ai)
names(pr)
#> [1] "desc_predictors" "regs_predictors"
table(pr$desc_predictors$type[pr$desc_predictors$category == "ALL"])
#> 
#>        <50 year-sector N             Expansionist             Missing info      Strategic (capital) 
#>                      120                        4                      109                      116 
#>       Strategic (labour)        Strategic (mixed) Strategic (productivity)         Transformational 
#>                      116                      117                      116                      120
reg <- pr$regs_predictors
knitr::kable(reg[reg$sample == "ALL" & reg$depvar == "HGE20" & grepl("^L3q4", reg$indepvar),
                 c("model", "controls", "indepvar", "b", "se", "obs")], digits = 3)
model controls indepvar b se obs
1 no L3q4_MFP_d 0.001 0.019 641
1 yes L3q4_MFP_d -0.006 0.019 641
3 no L3q4_avg_wage_d -0.009 0.017 738
3 no L3q4_phys_assets_d -0.007 0.017 738
3 yes L3q4_avg_wage_d -0.010 0.017 738
3 yes L3q4_phys_assets_d -0.010 0.017 738
1 no L3q4_MFP_d -0.011 0.020 430
1 yes L3q4_MFP_d -0.013 0.020 430
3 no L3q4_avg_wage_d 0.000 0.017 600
3 no L3q4_phys_assets_d -0.008 0.016 600
3 yes L3q4_avg_wage_d 0.001 0.018 600
3 yes L3q4_phys_assets_d -0.006 0.017 600
1 no L3q4_MFP_d -0.019 0.024 362
1 yes L3q4_MFP_d -0.014 0.024 362
3 no L3q4_avg_wage_d -0.006 0.025 420
3 no L3q4_phys_assets_d -0.023 0.023 420
3 yes L3q4_avg_wage_d -0.011 0.026 420
3 yes L3q4_phys_assets_d -0.023 0.024 420

The L3q4_* terms are dummies for the top quartile at t-3; desc_predictors describes the scalers of each type, regs_predictors holds every coefficient of every model.

Step 9: The scaler analysis

The scaler analysis looks more closely at the scalers of step 4.

Top scalers. compute_top_scalers() ranks the employment (HGE20) and turnover (HGT20) scalers of each year on three measures of growth from t-3 to t: relative growth (rel), absolute growth (abs) and the Birch-Schreyer index (bs, a mix of both). It keeps the top 50 and the top 1, 5, 10 and 25 % and describes each group in the format of step 5, with its share in job and turnover creation.

top <- compute_top_scalers(cfg, ai)
x <- top[top$year == 2019 & top$category == "ALL" &
           top$sample %in% c("HGE20_ranked", "HGE20_abs_p25", "HGE20_abs_p10"),
         c("sample", "firm_count", "median_L3employment", "median_employment",
           "share_creation_employment")]
knitr::kable(x, digits = 2)
sample firm_count median_L3employment median_employment share_creation_employment
HGE20_ranked 39 28.88 58.74 0.23
HGE20_abs_p10 4 128.05 314.25 0.08
HGE20_abs_p25 10 85.16 186.42 0.14

HGE20_ranked are all the ranked scalers, HGE20_abs_p10 the top 10 % by absolute growth. joint_growth = TRUE also requires the other variable (turnover for employment scalers) to grow.

Scalers to mid-caps. compute_midcap_transitions() follows scalers, the non-scalers of their pool and the top scalers from the start of their growth period (t-3), and records when they cross out of the SME category, with exit as a competing outcome. Three definitions are reported side by side:

  • small_midcap: EU small mid-cap (Recommendation (EU) 2025/1099: under 750 persons and turnover up to EUR 150 m or balance sheet up to EUR 129 m); firms that jump past these ceilings are counted separately as “to large”;
  • sme_exit: leaving the EU SME category, up to 3,000 employees;
  • employment_250: reaching 250 employees, the definition that does not need financial data.
mc <- compute_midcap_transitions(cfg, ai)
names(mc)
#> [1] "incidence" "entry"     "by_year"   "coverage"  "hazard"
inc <- mc$incidence
x <- inc[inc$definition == "employment_250" & inc$category == "ALL" & inc$step == 5 &
           inc$sample %in% c("HGE20", "HGE20_nonscaler_pool"),
         c("sample", "step", "at_risk", "cif_mid", "cif_exit")]
knitr::kable(x, digits = 3)
sample step at_risk cif_mid cif_exit
HGE20 5 108 0.066 0.144
HGE20_nonscaler_pool 5 1078 0.012 0.176

cif_mid is the cumulative share of firms that have crossed by that many years after entry, cif_exit the share that exited first. The other tables give the entries into the risk set (entry), crossings by calendar year (by_year), the coverage of the financial data (coverage), and a hazard model of crossing, with scalers compared with their pool (hazard):

hz <- mc$hazard
knitr::kable(hz[hz$term == "scaler" & hz$definition == "employment_250",
                c("sample", "window", "odds_ratio", "pval", "firms", "events")], digits = 3)
sample window odds_ratio pval firms events
HGE20 vs HGE20_nonscaler_pool from_t-3 1.366 0.535 1339 32
HGE20 vs HGE20_nonscaler_pool after_window 0.587 0.399 1198 21
HGT20 vs HGT20_nonscaler_pool from_t-3 2.786 0.008 1339 36
HGT20 vs HGT20_nonscaler_pool after_window 0.572 0.276 1198 21

Every variant (cut-offs, growth measures, definitions, the hazard from t-3 and after the growth period) is written, so the choice among them is left to the analysis.

Step 10: Confidentiality

The tables hold aggregates only, and medians are approximate (step 5). With dominance = TRUE in the configuration, each table also gets dom_<var> columns: the share of a cell’s total held by its largest dom_num firms, the statistic of the dominance rule. dominance_share() computes it for one cell:

emp_2019 <- ai$employment[ai$year == 2019 & ai$HGE20 %in% 1]
dominance_share(emp_2019, top_n = 2)
#> [1] 0.198669

Cells are not blanked automatically. Which cells to suppress before the tables leave the institute is the decision of the national statistical institute; the package reports the statistics needed for it.

Step 11: Running everything from files

In production, the input files are .dta files in input_dir, named as in vignette("input-data"), together with the reference files tl3_typology.dta (for region_3d) and exchange_rates.dta (for non-euro countries). With the example data:

dir <- "path/to/input"
haven::write_dta(ex$base_financials, file.path(dir, "base_financials_FR.dta"))
haven::write_dta(ex$plants_raw, file.path(dir, "plants_RAW_FR.dta"))
haven::write_dta(tl3_typology, file.path(dir, "tl3_typology.dta"))

cfg <- config_scaleup(country = "FR", input_dir = dir, output_dir = "path/to/output",
                      nace_revision = "2")
check_inputs(cfg)          # step 3
run_scaleup_pipeline(cfg)  # steps 4 to 8
run_scaler_analysis(cfg)   # step 9

run_scaleup_pipeline() writes the indicator panel accounts_indicators_FR.dta back to input_dir and the tables n13_<table>_FR.csv to output_dir; run_scaler_analysis() reads the panel and writes sa_<table>_FR.csv.

Optional: trade

The trade part adds firm-level trade in goods: the transaction-level file trade_RAW_<CT>.dta (see vignette("input-trade-data")) is summed per firm and year and merged onto the panel.

tai <- build_trade_accounts_indicators(cfg, ex$base_financials, ex$trade_raw, ex$plants_raw,
                                       tl3_typology = tl3_typology)
round(100 * tapply(tai$exporter, tai$year, mean, na.rm = TRUE), 1)
#> 2010 2011 2012 2013 2014 2015 2016 2017 2018 2019 2020 2021 2022 
#> 20.9 21.4 21.3 21.2 21.0 21.0 21.0 21.8 21.6 22.1 21.1 21.0 21.0

Among the turnover scalers, HGX20 marks the heavy exporting scalers, whose export growth is at least half of the turnover growth that makes a scaler, and HGNX20 the light exporting ones. compute_trade_characteristics() describes them in the format of step 5:

tc <- compute_trade_characteristics(cfg, tai)
x <- tc$p2[tc$p2$year == 2019 & tc$p2$category == "ALL",
           c("sample", "firm_count", "median_exp_value", "share_HGX")]
knitr::kable(x, digits = 2)
sample firm_count median_exp_value share_HGX
HGE10 30 1007.57 0.27
HGT10 39 1110.61 0.31
HGET10 47 1161.66 0.26
HGE20 4 1917.27 0.50
HGT20 7 1655.59 0.29
HGET20 8 1233.26 0.25

From files, run_trade_pipeline(cfg) does the same with trade_RAW_FR.dta in input_dir and writes trade_accounts_indicators_FR.dta and n16_trade_characteristics_*.csv. When that panel exists, run_scaler_analysis() uses it and adds the exporter breakdown.
